outputs.L1: We present high-resolution, high-sensitivity Very Large Array (VLA) observations of the 21 cm H I line emission from the face-on galaxy NGC 1058, providing the first reliable study of H I profile shapes across the entire disk of an external galaxy. Our observations reveal an intriguing view of the interstellar medium: throughout the galaxy, velocity dispersions range from 4 to 15 km s⁻¹, yet they show no correlation with star formation, stellar distribution, or gaseous spiral arms. Although the velocity dispersions decrease with radius, this global trend exhibits substantial scatter, including several isolated, spatially resolved regions of high dispersion. The radial decline in starlight is much steeper than either the decline in velocity dispersion or that of the energy associated with gas motions.
outputs.L2: Using high-resolution, highly sensitive Very Large Array (VLA) observations of 21 cm HI line emission from the nearly face-on galaxy NGC 1058, we provide the first dependable analysis of HI profile shapes across the full disk of an external galaxy. The data reveal a striking view of its interstellar medium: velocity dispersions across the galaxy span roughly 4 to 15 km/s, yet they show no clear connection with star formation, stellar distributions, or gaseous spiral arms. Although the dispersions generally become smaller at larger radii, this overall decrease includes substantial scatter, with several distinct, spatially resolved areas exhibiting unusually high dispersion. Starlight fades with radius far more rapidly than either the velocity dispersions or the energy associated with gas motions.

The study presents high-resolution, high-sensitivity Very Large Array (VLA) observations of 21 cm neutral hydrogen (H I) line emission from the nearly face-on galaxy NGC 1058. Because of the galaxy’s favorable orientation and the quality of the data, the observations make it possible to examine the shapes of H I line profiles across the disk in exceptional detail.

These data provide the first reliable study of H I profile shapes over the full disk of an external galaxy. By measuring the line profiles at many positions, the study is able to investigate how the motions of neutral gas vary from place to place and how these motions relate to other galactic structures and processes.

The measured H I velocity dispersions throughout NGC 1058 range from about 4 to 15 km s⁻¹. These dispersions show no clear correlation with regions of star formation, the distribution of stellar light, or the presence of gaseous spiral arms. This suggests that the processes responsible for driving or maintaining the observed gas motions are not simply tied to local star-forming activity or to the visible stellar and spiral structure of the galaxy.

Overall, the velocity dispersion tends to decrease with increasing radius from the center of NGC 1058. However, this radial decline is not smooth. There is considerable scatter in the measurements, caused in part by isolated regions where the gas shows unusually high velocity dispersion compared with its surroundings.

The study also finds that the stellar light decreases with radius much more rapidly than either the H I velocity dispersion or the kinetic energy associated with gas motions. In other words, while the stellar disk becomes faint relatively quickly at large radii, significant gas motions persist farther out in the galaxy. This difference places important constraints on possible energy sources for the turbulence and random motions observed in the neutral interstellar medium.

High-resolution, high-sensitivity observations with the Very Large Array (VLA) of the 21 cm neutral hydrogen (H I) line in the nearby, nearly face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1058 provide a detailed view of the kinematics of its atomic gas disk. Because the galaxy is oriented almost face-on, the observed line profiles are especially useful for studying random and turbulent gas motions with relatively little confusion from large-scale rotational velocities along the line of sight. These data make it possible to examine the shapes of H I emission profiles and to measure the velocity dispersion of the neutral gas across essentially the full extent of the galaxy’s disk.

The H I line profiles in NGC 1058 are not uniform from place to place. In many regions they show a relatively narrow central component, while in others broader wings or more complex profile shapes are present. By fitting and analyzing these profiles, the velocity dispersion of the atomic gas is found to range from about 4 to 15 km/s. The largest dispersions generally occur in the inner disk, while lower dispersions are more common at larger galactocentric radii. Overall, the H I velocity dispersion declines with radius, indicating that the atomic gas becomes dynamically colder in the outer parts of the galaxy.

A key result is that these variations in gas velocity dispersion do not show a strong local correlation with obvious tracers of stellar activity or disk structure. Regions of enhanced star formation do not consistently correspond to regions with higher H I velocity dispersion. Similarly, the velocity dispersion does not closely follow the distribution of the old stellar population or the locations of gaseous spiral arms. This lack of a clear spatial association suggests that the processes responsible for maintaining the observed gas motions are not simply the direct, local injection of energy from young stars, supernovae, stellar winds, or spiral-arm compression.

Instead, the results imply that other mechanisms may play an important role in driving or sustaining turbulence in the neutral interstellar medium of NGC 1058. Possible contributors include large-scale gravitational instabilities, energy input from differential rotation, magnetorotational effects, accretion of gas from outside the disk, or turbulence generated over broad spatial scales rather than by localized star-forming regions. The persistence of significant H I velocity dispersions even in regions with little current star formation indicates that the atomic gas disk is dynamically active throughout the galaxy.

Thus, the VLA observations of NGC 1058 show that the neutral hydrogen disk has a radially declining but still substantial level of random motion, with velocity dispersions of roughly 4–15 km/s. The absence of a strong connection between these motions and local star formation, stellar density, or spiral structure suggests that H I turbulence in this galaxy is maintained by processes that operate on large scales or are not directly tied to present-day stellar feedback.

The **Very Large Array** is one of the most famous radio astronomy observatories in the world. Located in New Mexico, USA, it consists of 27 large radio antennas arranged in a Y-shaped pattern across the desert. Each antenna is 25 meters wide, and together they work as one powerful telescope.

The purpose of the Very Large Array is to collect radio waves from space. Unlike optical telescopes, which observe visible light, the Very Large Array studies radio signals emitted by planets, stars, galaxies, black holes, and clouds of gas. This allows scientists to explore objects and events that may be invisible to ordinary telescopes.

One of the most important features of the Very Large Array is its size. The antennas can be moved along railroad tracks, changing the distance between them. When spread far apart, they provide very detailed images of distant objects. When placed closer together, they can detect larger and fainter structures in space.

The Very Large Array has contributed to many discoveries in astronomy. It has helped researchers study the center of the Milky Way, observe exploding stars, map distant galaxies, and investigate powerful jets from black holes. It has also appeared in popular culture, including movies and documentaries, making it a recognizable symbol of space science.

Overall, the Very Large Array is a remarkable tool for exploring the universe. By listening to radio waves from deep space, it helps scientists better understand the structure, history, and mysteries of the cosmos.

counterfactuals.output:
We present Very Large Array 21 cm H I observations of the nearly face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1058 aimed at characterizing the shapes of the atomic gas line profiles and the distribution of velocity dispersion across its disk. The low inclination of NGC 1058 minimizes rotational broadening along the line of sight, making it a useful laboratory for studying local H I kinematics and turbulent motions in galactic disks. We construct H I data cubes at multiple angular and velocity resolutions and examine both individual spectra and azimuthally averaged radial trends.

The H I profiles are generally well described by a narrow, approximately Gaussian core, but many lines of sight show asymmetric wings, excess broad emission, or multiple components, indicating that a single velocity dispersion does not fully capture the kinematic structure of the neutral interstellar medium. Gaussian fitting and moment analyses show that the characteristic H I velocity dispersion is of order several km s⁻¹ throughout the disk, with typical values near 6–10 km s⁻¹. The dispersion is largest in the inner disk and in regions of enhanced H I structure, and declines gradually with radius, although significant local variations remain at all radii. In the outer disk, where star formation is weak, the H I profiles retain measurable nonthermal widths, suggesting that mechanisms in addition to local stellar feedback may contribute to maintaining the observed gas motions.

We find that profile shape varies systematically across the galaxy: high-column-density regions often exhibit complex or broadened profiles, while lower-column-density outer regions tend to show narrower and more symmetric lines. The presence of broad wings and multi-component spectra implies a mixture of cold and warm neutral gas, unresolved bulk motions, or localized expanding structures. These results demonstrate that even in a nearly face-on system, H I line widths reflect a combination of thermal broadening, turbulence, and small-scale dynamical structure. NGC 1058 therefore provides an important benchmark for interpreting H I velocity dispersions in spiral galaxies and for assessing the energy sources that sustain turbulence in the atomic interstellar medium.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an astrophysics-style summary describing the first reliable study of HI profile shapes across an external galaxy disk using VLA data for NGC 1058.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a VLA study of the shapes of neutral hydrogen 21-cm line profiles across the disk of the nearly face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1058, providing one of the first reliable spatially resolved measurements of H I profile structure in an external galaxy. The low inclination of NGC 1058 minimizes rotational broadening and line-of-sight projection effects, allowing the observed profiles to be interpreted primarily in terms of local interstellar gas motions rather than large-scale galactic kinematics.

The H I emission is mapped over the optical and outer disk with sufficient angular and spectral resolution to examine variations in line width, asymmetry, and non-Gaussian structure as a function of position. Across much of the disk, the profiles are well described by relatively narrow components with characteristic velocity dispersions of order several km s⁻¹, but many regions show significant departures from a single Gaussian form. These include asymmetric profiles, extended wings, and multiple-component features, indicating that the atomic medium is dynamically complex even in a quiescent, face-on system.

The profile shapes vary systematically across the galaxy. Broader and more structured profiles are preferentially associated with regions of enhanced H I column density and recent star formation, suggesting that stellar feedback, expanding shells, turbulence, and localized bulk motions contribute to the observed line broadening. In contrast, the outer disk generally exhibits narrower and more regular profiles, consistent with a lower level of mechanical energy input and a cooler or less turbulent H I layer.

Because beam smearing from differential rotation is small in NGC 1058, the measured line widths provide a robust estimate of the internal velocity field of the atomic gas. The results demonstrate that H I profile shapes contain information beyond simple column density and velocity maps, revealing the mixture of thermal, turbulent, and organized motions within the disk. This VLA study of NGC 1058 therefore establishes a foundation for using resolved 21-cm profile analysis as a diagnostic of the structure and energetics of the neutral interstellar medium in external galaxies.
